title: Milk Quality and Mastitis Management — Todd Meyer DVM (US Grains Council Thailand, March 2024)
provenance_note: Image-dominant original PowerPoint; slide text is a concise visually reviewed summary, not a verbatim reproduction. Numerical examples from historical slides are educational and not universal clinical advice.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text: Introduction. Milk Quality and Mastitis Management; Todd Meyer DVM, Dairy Health and Management Consulting; US Grains Council Thailand, March 2024. Milker training content credited to Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine.

pages.title: Good management
pages.text: Good management. Milk quality and production are affected by health, nutrition, people, reproduction and housing. The illustration shows these management factors contributing to milk.

pages.title: Milk letdown
pages.text: Milk letdown. Oxytocin stimulates myoepithelial muscle contraction surrounding the mammary alveoli, causing milk letdown.

pages.title: Milk letdown stimuli
pages.text: Milk letdown stimuli. Touching or preparing the udder provides sensory stimulation associated with oxytocin release and milk letdown.

pages.title: Neural pathway for milk letdown
pages.text: Neural pathway for milk letdown. Udder stimulation sends nerve signals to the brain and pituitary gland.

pages.title: Oxytocin pathway
pages.text: Oxytocin pathway. Oxytocin travels via the bloodstream to the udder; the slide notes it remains in the blood for only a short time.

pages.title: Milk letdown inhibition
pages.text: Milk letdown inhibition. Inadequate udder preparation, too much delay before attaching milking machines, fear or pain such as yelling or hitting can inhibit milk letdown.

pages.title: Cow behavior and routine
pages.text: Cow behavior and routine. Cows are creatures of habit. Maintain consistent routines and avoid rapid movements and loud noises.

pages.title: Cow blind spot
pages.text: Cow blind spot. Approach cows within their area of sight. Let the cow know someone is approaching; diagram labels a blind area.

pages.title: Milking routine overview
pages.text: Milking routine overview. The milking routine consists of gloves and hygiene, teat preparation, forestripping, cleaning/drying, milking unit attachment, removal and post-milking disinfection. Each step matters for cow health and milk.

pages.title: Teat preparation sequence and timing
pages.text: Teat preparation sequence and timing. Diagram shows pre-dip, stripping all four quarters, cleaning and drying teats, and attaching the milking unit. Timing labels include 30 seconds and 90 seconds in the preparation sequence.

pages.title: Pre-dipping disinfectant coverage
pages.text: Pre-dipping disinfectant coverage. Pre-dipping disinfects teats before milking. Cover about three quarters of the teat; leave disinfectant on 30 seconds. Spray and dip can both be effective.

pages.title: Correct pre-dip coverage
pages.text: Correct pre-dip coverage. Visuals compare no dip or incorrect dipping with correct teat coverage; incomplete coverage leaves contamination at the teat orifice.

pages.title: Forestripping and mastitis detection
pages.text: Forestripping and mastitis detection. Strip and visually inspect approximately three squirts of milk from each teat to stimulate letdown and look for abnormal milk as a mastitis detection step.

pages.title: Wiping teats
pages.text: Wiping teats. Clean and dry teats completely, including the teat orifice; do not share towels between cows.

pages.title: Milking unit attachment
pages.text: Milking unit attachment. Attach the unit within 90 seconds after stimulation according to this lecture, ensure milk flows from all four quarters, and avoid overmilking.

pages.title: Post-milking teat dipping
pages.text: Post-milking teat dipping. Apply post-dip immediately after removing the milking unit; visual shows proper dip coverage.

pages.title: Milk quality components
pages.text: Milk quality components. High somatic cell counts due to mastitis and undesirable contaminants can damage milk quality. Examples include pesticides, detergents, added water, antibiotics and bacteria from mastitis or poor hygiene.

pages.title: Bacteria basics
pages.text: Bacteria basics. Bacteria are microorganisms found in many places; they multiply rapidly under suitable conditions of food, temperature and time.

pages.title: Bacteria entering udder
pages.text: Bacteria entering udder. Bacteria enter through the teat end; damage to the teat end raises likelihood of entry. Diagram shows teat canal closure and keratin plug protection.

pages.title: Healthy teat end
pages.text: Healthy teat end. Histology photo and close-up illustrate a healthy teat duct and keratin in the teat canal.

pages.title: Damaged teat end
pages.text: Damaged teat end. Histology and external close-up illustrate a damaged/frayed teat end, potentially compromising the barrier.

pages.title: Bacterial growth rate
pages.text: Bacterial growth rate. Lecture illustration states that under favorable conditions some bacteria can double every 10 to 20 minutes; this is conditional, not a universal growth rate.

pages.title: Bacteria sources in bulk tank
pages.text: Bacteria sources in bulk tank. Milk tank bacteria can come from milkers (dirt, wash problems, abnormal milk) or cows (contagious and environmental mastitis); cow hygiene and pre-milking preparation affect manure entry.

pages.title: Somatic cell count definition
pages.text: Somatic cell count definition. SCC is used as an indicator of milk quality and udder health. Somatic cells are mainly white blood cells that rise during infection. The lecture notes uninfected quarters generally have SCC below 100,000 cells/mL.

pages.title: High SCC and milk quality
pages.text: High SCC and milk quality. High SCC indicates lower milk quality, with effects on taste, shelf life and cheese processing yield according to the slide.

pages.title: Mastitis and elevated SCC
pages.text: Mastitis and elevated SCC. Udder infection/inflammation involves bacteria and increased somatic cells; diagram shows both near the teat duct.

pages.title: Definition and effects of mastitis
pages.text: Definition and effects of mastitis. Mastitis is inflammation of the udder, most often bacterial in the lecture. It may reduce milk production, alter milk quality/composition and present clinical illness.

pages.title: Clinical mastitis grades
pages.text: Clinical mastitis grades. Grade 1: abnormal milk only (watery, flakes, clots). Grade 2: abnormal milk plus udder inflammation, redness, pain or swelling. Grade 3: systemic sickness such as fever, weakness or diarrhea, with abnormal milk and potentially abnormal udder.

pages.title: Mastitis prevention
pages.text: Mastitis prevention. Keep teats clean and dry, milking equipment clean, disinfect teats, and maintain a clean, dry environment.

pages.title: California Mastitis Test overview
pages.text: California Mastitis Test overview. CMT is a cow-side screening test related to somatic cell count; useful for identifying cows with high SCC and tracking mastitis control.

pages.title: California Mastitis Test protocol
pages.text: California Mastitis Test protocol. 1 Clean teats, strip and discard 2–3 foremilk streams. 2 Collect about 10 mL from each teat in separate paddle compartments. 3 Add equal amount of CMT reagent. 4 Gently swirl in circles for about 10 seconds, observe and record results.

pages.title: CMT scores and SCC comparison
pages.text: CMT scores and SCC comparison. Lecture illustration lists CMT negative≈100,000 cells/mL; trace≈300,000; score 1≈900,000; score 2≈2,700,000; score 3≈8,100,000. Score 1 or more signals elevated likelihood of udder infection. These are illustrative estimates, not exact individual cow conversions.

pages.title: Bulk tank SCC and infection estimates
pages.text: Bulk tank SCC and infection estimates. Historical National Mastitis Council 2001 example estimates herd infection prevalence from bulk tank SCC: 200,000≈15%, 400,000≈33%, 700,000≈67%; approximately 8–10% more infected cows for each additional 100,000 SCC. Estimates are context dependent, not diagnostic percentages for an individual farm.

pages.title: Bulk tank SCC and infected quarters
pages.text: Bulk tank SCC and infected quarters. New Zealand 36-herd chart relates bulk tank SCC to prevalence of infected quarters (reported R²=0.47). SCC response varies with organism; high SCC is a herd-level signal rather than direct case count.

pages.title: SCC and cumulative milk loss
pages.text: SCC and cumulative milk loss. A chart from Canadian data (115,000 cows, 2,800 herds) illustrates rising cumulative milk losses as duration of elevated SCC increases across lactations.

pages.title: Daily milk loss by SCC
pages.text: Daily milk loss by SCC. Historical example table (Hand et al., 2012): lactation 1 low production SCC200k=0.35 kg/day loss, SCC600k=0.89; lactation1 high 0.80 vs 2.08; lactation2 low 0.61 vs 1.59; lactation2 high 1.07 vs 2.77; lactation3+ low 0.63 vs 1.63; lactation3+ high 1.09 vs 2.81. Illustrative study findings, not universal cow predictions.

pages.title: Clean milking equipment and dry cows
pages.text: Clean milking equipment and dry cows. Rinse visible manure from units and shake off excess water before attaching; do not directly wet udders before milking in the depicted milking routine.

pages.title: Examples of poor milking hygiene
pages.text: Examples of poor milking hygiene. Images show a shared cloth for udders, incompletely washed towels and water dripping from udder into teat cups as undesirable practices.

pages.title: Clean and dry bedding
pages.text: Clean and dry bedding. Provide sufficient bedding for comfort; add or change bedding frequently; remove manure frequently to keep stalls dry.

pages.title: Cow hygiene scoring
pages.text: Cow hygiene scoring. Illustrated cow hygiene scoring card uses scores 1–4 for udder, legs and flank/upper leg. Higher 3–4 scores are associated with greater udder infection risk.

pages.title: Environmental cow cleanliness review
pages.text: Environmental cow cleanliness review. Investigate dirty stalls, dirty travel lanes and dirt transfer patterns. Examine whether cows are dry and where manure contamination originates.

pages.title: Investigate dirty legs and udders
pages.text: Investigate dirty legs and udders. Walk cow travel path to and from parlor; look for puddles, broken concrete and clogged drainage; observe water cooling, shift end, heavy rain, and manure scraping conditions.

pages.title: Milking equipment cleaning and maintenance
pages.text: Milking equipment cleaning and maintenance. Residual milk in buckets, hoses and clusters supports bacterial growth. Use effective cleaning and proper agents for milk-contact surfaces; inspect and replace cracked or damaged rubber hoses and inflations.

pages.title: Continuous milk quality improvement
pages.text: Continuous milk quality improvement. Identify critical weaknesses, prioritize by impact and implementability, rank control strategies by cost, track progress, reassess and adjust plan.

pages.title: Global dairy trend
pages.text: Global dairy trend. Lecture suggests larger efficient operations, better milk quality for improved payment/customer satisfaction, greater production efficiency and economies of scale.

pages.title: National Mastitis Council 10-point plan
pages.text: National Mastitis Council 10-point plan. Ten topics: udder health goals; clean dry comfortable environment; proper milking; equipment maintenance; good records; lactating clinical mastitis management; effective dry cow management; contagious pathogen biosecurity; routine udder health monitoring; periodic program review.

pages.title: Mastitis treatment concepts
pages.text: Mastitis treatment concepts. Distinguishes bacteriological cure, clinical cure and changes in SCC. Clinical signs can resolve independently of bacterial cure. Lecture mentions recovery timing; do not assume treatment is always needed or choose drugs from this slide.

pages.title: Lecture mastitis treatment grades 1 and 2
pages.text: Lecture mastitis treatment grades 1 and 2. Slide discusses intramammary products, cases with abnormal milk, and grade 3 systemic illness requiring greater veterinary attention. It includes historical treatment suggestions; clinical treatment decisions and withdrawal requirements need a veterinarian and local protocols.

pages.title: Dry cow treatment overview
pages.text: Dry cow treatment overview. Dry-period management discusses selecting protocols using bulk tank SCC and herd risk, antibiotic dry cow treatment, internal teat sealants and prevention of new infections. Historical thresholds are contextual, not individual prescriptions.

pages.title: Dry cow therapy and teat sealant research
pages.text: Dry cow therapy and teat sealant research. Slides summarize research on reducing intramammary infections during dry periods using dry cow treatment and internal teat sealants; outcomes differ across studies and herds.

pages.title: Internal teat sealant meta-analysis
pages.text: Internal teat sealant meta-analysis. Research summary of 12 studies and 17 subtrials in more than 10,000 cows from over 130 herds compares internal teat sealant with antibiotic dry cow therapy. Study findings should not be generalized into one treatment protocol.

pages.title: Research findings for teat sealants
pages.text: Research findings for teat sealants. Raibee et al. (J Dairy Sci 96, 2013) research charts show relative reduction in intramammary infection and clinical mastitis with dry cow teat sealant comparisons, with benefits dependent on infection prevalence.

pages.title: Internal teat sealants application
pages.text: Internal teat sealants application. Diagram and image describe intramammary bismuth subnitrate sealant at dry-off to help prevent new infections; slide notes removal by hand stripping before first milking after calving. Application requires hygienic veterinary-approved protocol.

pages.title: Coliform mastitis vaccination
pages.text: Coliform mastitis vaccination. Slide mentions J-5 bacterin used as one control element for coliform mastitis; evidence described reduction in severity rather than necessarily infection incidence.

pages.title: Hot environments and mastitis risk
pages.text: Hot environments and mastitis risk. Heat stress weakens cow immune response; warm humid conditions favor bacterial growth. Wet bedding, water for cooling and travel lanes can contribute to poor hygiene and greater mastitis risk.

pages.title: Heat stress and respiration
pages.text: Heat stress and respiration. Slide emphasizes heat stress in transition cows, weakened immune responses and higher summer mastitis. Lecture describes normal respiration about 15–35/min and heat stress respiration above 60/min, context-dependent.

pages.title: Basic mastitis microbiology
pages.text: Basic mastitis microbiology. Slide depicts sterile milk collection after alcohol cleaning and standard laboratory blood agar culture, with subsequent identification tests. It describes incubation at 37°C for 24 h in the teaching demonstration; use current lab SOP and biosafety controls.

pages.title: Culture equipment and supplies
pages.text: Culture equipment and supplies. Slides show incubator, microscope, blood agar plates, optional MacConkey agar, loops, Gram stain reagents, 3% KOH, catalase reagent (3% H2O2), coagulase serum, gloves and sample vials.

pages.title: Mastitis diagnostic decision tree
pages.text: Mastitis diagnostic decision tree. Educational simplified pathogen identification tree: Gram stain or KOH → catalase → coagulase test for Staphylococcus aureus vs coagulase-negative staphylococci; Gram morphology differentiates cocci and rods. Confirm with validated laboratory methods.

pages.title: Gram stain and KOH interpretation
pages.text: Gram stain and KOH interpretation. Gram-positive bacteria stain violet and do not form KOH strings; Gram-negative bacteria stain red and may form viscous strings with KOH. Slide shows cocci versus rods under microscopy.

pages.title: Gram stain technique
pages.text: Gram stain technique. Slide illustrates crystal violet, iodine, alcohol decolorization and safranin counterstain; results differentiate gram-positive/gram-negative and rod/cocci morphology. Validate using lab SOP.

pages.title: Catalase test
pages.text: Catalase test. Catalase test with 3% hydrogen peroxide distinguishes catalase-positive staphylococci (bubbles) from catalase-negative streptococci in the depicted workflow.

pages.title: Coagulase and blood agar hemolysis
pages.text: Coagulase and blood agar hemolysis. Coagulase clot formation is illustrated as positive for Staph. aureus and negative for coagulase-negative staphylococci; blood agar demonstrates complete or partial hemolysis around colonies.

pages.title: Coagulase slide or tube test
pages.text: Coagulase slide or tube test. Slide illustrates coagulase serum agglutination/clot tests, using rabbit coagulase serum; illustrated slide and tube assays and observation of clotting. Confirm conditions using validated SOP.

pages.title: Specialized mastitis culture plates
pages.text: Specialized mastitis culture plates. The deck shows specialized selective culture plates (including tri-plate) for distinguishing pathogen groups using colony growth patterns; availability varies by market.

pages.title: Culture results interpretation
pages.text: Culture results interpretation. No growth after 48 hours can occur despite clinical signs. Discusses causative pathogens, multiple colony types suggesting contamination, overgrowth due to handling and importance of sample quality.

pages.title: Limitations of farm-based cultures
pages.text: Limitations of farm-based cultures. Some serious organisms are not easily detected. Mycoplasma may need special media and incubation; farm culture may not distinguish contagious Strep agalactiae from other streptococci or separate all gram-negative species.

pages.title: Herd survey using culture
pages.text: Herd survey using culture. Practical herd survey: screen cows with CMT and culture higher-scoring quarters, seek patterns of contagious pathogens versus environmental pathogens, inspect cleaning and milking weak points.

pages.title: Cultures and treatment decisions
pages.text: Cultures and treatment decisions. Milk cultures can help classify clinical mastitis, reveal herd pathogen patterns and guide selective treatment decisions. The lecture discusses withholding immediate treatment for some mild cases pending test results but treatment decisions need a veterinarian.

pages.title: Selective mastitis treatment
pages.text: Selective mastitis treatment. Overview of pathogen-informed selective therapy and importance of cow severity, gram category, no-growth results and local farm/veterinarian protocols. Do not infer antibiotic prescriptions from generic source.

pages.title: Typical mastitis culture results
pages.text: Typical mastitis culture results. Illustrative chart reports 25–30% no growth, 25–30% gram-negative and 40–50% gram-positive among selected clinical mastitis cases. Historical study mix; not universal farm prevalence.

pages.title: Culture-based treatment protocols
pages.text: Culture-based treatment protocols. Slide describes sampling mild/moderate cases for culture, prompt attention to severe cases and culture results after 24–36 hours; discusses reducing antibiotic use and discarded milk, requiring farm-specific veterinary protocol.

pages.title: Spontaneous bacteriological cure rates
pages.text: Spontaneous bacteriological cure rates. Lecture literature table (Ruegg AABP 2017): Staph aureus 0–11%; Streptococci 28–30%; coagulase-negative staphylococci 44–66%; E. coli 80–95%; Klebsiella 25–60%; no-growth 75–85%. Study-dependent estimates, not predictions for individual cows.

pages.title: Antibiotic benefits and limits
pages.text: Antibiotic benefits and limits. Research slide estimates 22–33% of selected cases benefit from antibiotic treatment in a specific scenario and warns treatment benefit can be overestimated; case-specific interpretation required.

pages.title: Clinical cure and treatment course
pages.text: Clinical cure and treatment course. Slide notes many mild/moderate cases recover apparent milk abnormalities within days regardless of antibiotic therapy; clinical cure is not identical to bacteriological cure and routine second courses may not be warranted without reassessment.

pages.title: Closing and contacts
pages.text: Closing and contacts. Final slide thanks hosts and sponsors, and invites questions. No additional technical material.
